name: block-aligner
baseline: parasail (C), ksw2 ksw_extz2_sse (C), Edlib (C++), WFA2-lib (C), each called from the Rust benchmark through FFI bindings (parasailors, ksw2-sys, edlib_rs, rust-wfa2)
workload: Global affine-gap alignment with traceback of Illumina reads, Nanopore reads (1 kbp, under 10 kbp, under 50 kbp) with match 2, mismatch -4, gap open -6, extend -2, plus Uniclust30 protein pairs (BLOSUM62, gaps 11/1) and SCOP sequence-to-profile pairs against score-only parasail.
claimed_speedup: Saved notebook outputs in vis/block_aligner_bench_vis.ipynb, total seconds, 'ours (1%-1%)' with traceback vs baselines: Illumina 0.331 s vs Edlib 1.078, ksw_extz2_sse(1%) 0.702, ksw_extz2_sse(10%) 0.662, parasail 1.877, WFA2 0.0396, WFA2 adaptive 0.0338; Nanopore 1kbp 0.355 vs Edlib 0.982, ksw2(1%) 0.690, ksw2(10%) 1.492, WFA2 1.074, WFA2 adaptive 0.968, parasail 4.241; Nanopore under 10kbp 1.233 vs Edlib 4.182, ksw2(1%) 2.041, ksw2(10%) 13.948, WFA2 12.232, WFA2 adaptive 2.636, parasail 35.789; Nanopore under 50kbp 29.619 vs Edlib 63.197, ksw2(1%) 44.493, ksw2(10%) 571.018, WFA2 331.475, WFA2 adaptive 58.830 (parasail not run). Derived from page data: block-aligner is 2.1x to 3.4x faster than Edlib, 1.5x to 2.1x faster than banded ksw2 at 1% band, 5.7x to 29x faster than parasail, but about 8.4x SLOWER than exact WFA2 on Illumina reads. Protein Uniclust30 (no traceback) 0.0886 s vs parasail 0.8250 s (9.3x, derived); with traceback 0.1698 s (4.9x, derived). SCOP profile pairs 0.149 s (block 32-32) vs parasail 0.597 s (4.0x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: cargo run --release --features simd_avx2 on Rust nightly (rust-toolchain file says 'nightly'); Cargo profile.release lto='thin', panic='abort'; the DNA script sets CC=/usr/local/opt/llvm/bin/clang for the C/C++ -sys crates; their optimisation flags live in each -sys crate's build script and were not read; rustc and clang versions unstated.
hardware: CPU model not stated anywhere opened; AVX2 build; notebook paths (/usr/local/anaconda3, Homebrew LLVM clang) suggest an x86-64 macOS machine.
tradeoffs: Heuristic, not exact: the block shifts, grows and shrinks greedily, so it can return a suboptimal score (README: 'at the expense of some accuracy'); block size must be tuned (README: min 32, max 256 for proteins; about 1% and 10% of length for Nanopore reads); 16-bit lanes saturate on very large scores; the SIMD instruction set (SSE2, AVX2, Neon, WASM SIMD) is chosen by Cargo feature at compile time with no runtime detection; tests and benchmarks need nightly Rust; C API available in c/.
caveats: The Bioinformatics paper (Liu and Steinegger 2023) could not be opened (doi, PMC and bioRxiv are blocked here), so the numbers come from the repo's executed benchmark notebook, which the README says reproduces the manuscript experiments; a search-result snippet of the paper abstract says 5-10x faster than some previous methods with under 3% error on protein and long-read data (not verified on the page). Not like-for-like: block-aligner is an approximate aligner while Edlib (unit-cost edit distance), parasail and WFA2 without heuristic are exact and use different scoring models, and ksw2 is banded; the parasail rows use score-only global_alignment_score (no traceback) in the protein benchmark and, in the DNA global benchmark, parasail is likewise score-only while block-aligner and the others compute a path, which favours parasail; the speedup over parasail grows with length because parasail does full O(nm) DP. WFA2 is far faster than block-aligner on low-error short reads. The C/C++ baselines are reached through forked binding crates (parasailors-new, edlib-rs with logging removed, rust-wfa2 fork with 'small changes that ensures wfa2 code autovectorizes', ksw2-sys), so call overhead and build flags may differ from stock builds. Single saved run, no error bars; datasets must be downloaded separately (data/README.md). Lead came from the A*PA2 enricher (pa-bench lists block-aligner as an approximate aligner); the pa-bench result files were not reachable.
found_via: seed-record pass: github.com/Daniel-Liu-c0deb0t/block-aligner README, examples/nanopore_bench_global.rs, Cargo.toml and vis/block_aligner_bench_vis.ipynb via raw.githubusercontent.com
why_faster: Adaptive block-based dynamic programming: only a small square block is computed and shifted down or right greedily (growing or shrinking as needed) instead of the full matrix or a fixed band, using SIMD; the README says this trades some accuracy for speed.

name: triple_accel
baseline: none measured: the README and benches compare only against the crate's own scalar fallback; no edlib (C++) or parasail (C) comparison found
workload: Hamming and Levenshtein distance and search on random strings (criterion benches), SIMD routines against the crate's own naive scalar versions.
claimed_speedup: README: vectorized SIMD code 'allows for up to 20-30x speedups over their scalar counterparts' (a general statement against the crate's own scalar routines, not a table and not a C/C++ baseline). No numeric comparison against edlib or parasail in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: README recommends RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native'; Cargo release profile opt-level=3, codegen-units=1, panic='abort'; benches use criterion 0.3.
tradeoffs: u8 byte strings only (no Unicode); x86 and x86-64 only for the SIMD paths (AVX2 and SSE4.1, runtime-detected), other CPUs fall back to scalar; the SIMD element width and vector type are selected at runtime from the input lengths.
caveats: No C/C++ comparison in the repo (benches/rand_benchmarks.rs compares only hamming_naive, levenshtein_naive and the crate's SIMD routines). The only cross-implementation timing found is inside block-aligner's own notebook (Rust against Rust): triple_accel 7,809,720 ns for the 1000/10000 nucleotide case against 226,318 ns for block-aligner (about 34x slower, derived from page data) and 23,337 ns against 23,150 ns for the 100/1000 case. A web search found no third-party edlib or parasail benchmark; the pa-bench harness (pairwise-alignment/pa-bench) wraps triple_accel next to edlib and parasail but its published result files were not reachable. Notable only by usage (109 stars); recorded at D per the seed-record instruction.
found_via: seed-record pass: github.com/Daniel-Liu-c0deb0t/triple_accel README and benches/rand_benchmarks.rs; cross-checked against vis/block_aligner_bench_vis.ipynb in block-aligner
why_faster: SIMD vectorisation (AVX2 or SSE4.1) of Hamming and Levenshtein routines with the vector width chosen from the string lengths; the README ties the 20-30x figure only to the scalar fallback.

name: ish
baseline: parasail (C) parasail_aligner, striped semi-global (sg_dx_striped sse41_128 and avx2_256, 8- and 16-bit variants)
workload: Single-thread semi-global search of one 23 bp DNA pattern (ACTCGACTTCAGCTACGCACATA) across the human T2T CHM13 v2.0 genome (chm13v2.0.fa), ish scoring match 2, mismatch -2, gap open 3, extend 1.
claimed_speedup: Sassy evals README (written by the authors of a competing tool): ish takes 69 s with an SSE build and 110 s with the AVX2 build; parasail_aligner with ish's cost parameters (-X 2 -M 2 -o 3 -e 1) takes '81s-198s' across the four striped variants (sse41_128_8, sse41_128_16, avx2_256_8, avx2_256_16); with parasail's default cost parameters it takes '53-69s'. Best against best at matched costs: 81 s / 69 s = 1.17x faster (derived from page data); the per-variant mapping of times is not given. The ish README itself gives no performance numbers.
compiler_and_flags: ish: 'mojo build --march native' via pixi (HEAD pins Mojo 0.25.6; the Sassy comparison used ish commit 92f4fad of 2025-07-21, whose Mojo version is probably 25.4 per the CHANGELOG), SSE row built with -D ISH_SIMD_TARGET=sse; parasail: built from a git clone with its default configure or cmake build, flags not stated.
tradeoffs: CLI grep-like record filter written in Mojo (pixi or conda install); striped semi-global and local alignment with affine gaps and scoring matrices; optional GPU path; SIMD width is a compile-time choice (SSE or AVX2 or AVX-512); ish-aligner is flagged development-only.
caveats: The paper the README links (bioRxiv 10.1101/2025.06.04.657890) could not be opened (host blocked), so the authors' own parasail numbers are unseen; the only numbers found are from the Sassy repo, where Sassy's authors time ish and parasail as side baselines. CPU model, Mojo and parasail build flags and run count are not given in that README. The win depends on cost parameters: parasail with its default costs (53-69 s) is as fast as or faster than ish (69 s SSE, 110 s AVX2). The ish AVX2 build is slower than SSE for this short pattern. The repo ships a reproducible harness (benchmarking/bench_scripts/bench.py, 'pixi run bench-all-cpu', uniprot_sprot 2015_11 and the parasail paper's query set, parasail built with autoreconf and configure) but no stored results. Lead came from the Sassy evaluations; no ksw2 comparison found.

name: banzai
baseline: bzip2 reference implementation (C); lbzip2 and pbzip2 not compared
workload: bzip2 compression (encoder only; no decompressor) using a linear-time SA-IS suffix array for the Burrows-Wheeler transform; the README gives only a qualitative runtime comparison with no numbers.
claimed_speedup: None. README: 'Compared to the reference implementation, banzai has worse average runtime but better worst-case runtime'; compression ratios 'very similar'; unchecked indexing 'could be approximately 10% faster' (no data).
tradeoffs: Entirely safe Rust; alpha software ('not battle-hardened'); encoder only (use bzip2-rs to decompress); runs SA-IS on the input concatenated with itself because bzip2 uses a wrap-around BWT; level 1-9 block size as in bzip2; bnz command-line tool mimics bzip(1).
caveats: Not a faster-than-C claim: the author states the average runtime is worse than the C reference and only the worst case (pathological inputs) is better, with no measurements in the README, repo tree (bnz, debug, fuzz, lib) or crate docs. The newest commit (2026-07-28) only bumps the Rust edition; the previous commit is from 2022-09-26. Notable only by usage; recorded at D per the seed-record instruction.

why_faster: Linear-time SA-IS suffix-array construction for the BWT removes the worst case of bzip2's block sorting; the author says average runtime is still worse.

name: reed-solomon-simd
baseline: catid/leopard (C++) and Intel ISA-L erasure code (C): neither compared; README compares only against Rust crates
workload: Reed-Solomon encode and decode over GF(2^16) with 1024-byte shards, 32:32 up to 57344:8192 original:recovery shard counts, single core AVX2.
claimed_speedup: No C or C++ comparison. Absolute README numbers (single core AVX2, AMD Ryzen 5 3600, MiB/s or GiB/s over original plus recovery shards): encode 32:32 10.237 GiB/s, 128:128 7.3891 GiB/s, 1024:1024 4.8495 GiB/s, 32768:32768 1.6049 GiB/s; decode (1% loss) 32:32 254.24 MiB/s, 1024:1024 1.3017 GiB/s. README says the crate 'is the fastest in all cases' against the Rust crates reed-solomon-16, reed-solomon-erasure, reed-solomon-novelpoly and leopard-codec on that Ryzen, except decoding with about 42 or fewer recovery shards.
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench main (criterion 0.7) and cargo run --release --example quick-comparison; runtime SIMD selection (AVX2, SSSE3, Neon, plain Rust fallback); rustc version and RUSTFLAGS unstated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 3600 (Zen 2); README adds Apple M1 about the same (+-10%)
tradeoffs: O(n log n) Leopard-RS algorithm in GF(2^16): 1 to 32768 original and recovery shards (up to 65535 with limits), shard length must be even; no error detection inside shards; unsafe only for the SSSE3, AVX2 and Neon engines; a fork of reed-solomon-16 by Markus Laire, itself based on catid/leopard (BSD-3-Clause portion).
caveats: Lead asked for a comparison with catid/leopard (C++) or ISA-L; none in the README, CHANGELOG or examples/quick-comparison.rs. catid/leopard's Benchmarks.md gives MB/s on an unstated 'few year old laptop' with 64 KB pieces, 128:128 Input=1964.98 MB/s encode, which cannot be compared with this crate's 1024-byte-shard Ryzen figures (different shard size, hardware and byte accounting; 'not very rigorous' by its author), so no ratio is derived. The 'fastest' claim is first-party and covers Rust crates only. A web search found no head-to-head with Leopard C++ or ISA-L.

name: go-cv-simd
baseline: OpenCV 2.4.x (C and C++; cvSmooth and cvSobel C API) called through go-opencv (cgo bindings, lazywei/go-opencv)
workload: Go testing benchmarks (ns/op) on a square Resolution x Resolution 8-bit image: 3x3 Gaussian, 3x3 box blur, 3x3 and 5x5 median, each for 1 channel (gray) and 3 channels (RGB); SSE2 kernels only.
claimed_speedup: README: -61.21% to -85.08% ns/op against go-opencv. Gaussian 74338 to 18481 ns (-75.14%), GaussianRGB 186024 to 57169 (-69.27%), Blur 110155 to 16623 (-84.91%), BlurRGB 293017 to 53716 (-81.67%), Median3x3 129268 to 23270 (-82.00%), Median3x3RGB 169857 to 65896 (-61.21%), Median5x5 883311 to 131812 (-85.08%), Median5x5RGB 1246845 to 388415 (-68.85%). About 2.6x to 6.7x faster (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain version unstated; assembly generated by c2goasm from clang-compiled SimdSse2*.cpp.s files of the C++ Simd library (sse2/sse2.sh); OpenCV build and flags unstated, version 2.4.10 per a comment in sse2/benchmarks_opencv_test.go.
hardware: not stated (the '-8' suffix in the benchmark names means GOMAXPROCS=8); the build script paths point to the author's macOS machine
tradeoffs: Go assembly auto-translated from compiled C++ (not hand-written Go); x86-64 SSE2 numbers only (sse2, ssse3 and avx2 directories exist, ARM absent); the companion go-cv wrapper is described as work in progress; requires keeping the c2goasm-generated .s files in sync with Simd.
caveats: This is effectively evidence for the C++ Simd library (ermig1979/Simd, compiled by clang) against a 2017-era OpenCV 2.4 Smooth path, not a claim about Go; the Go side only calls generated assembly. Image size (the Resolution constant), CPU, Go version and OpenCV build are unstated, and the Resolution value was not found in the files opened. The OpenCV rows are cgo calls through go-opencv, so a small per-call cgo cost is part of the baseline, though the smallest timed row is 16,623 ns so it is probably minor; OpenCV 2.x is long superseded and newer releases likely have faster SIMD paths for these filters (not measured here), so the ratios may not hold today. First-party numbers, no repeat counts.

why_faster: Hand-written SSE2 intrinsic kernels of the Simd library (compiled from C++ and embedded as Go assembly) against OpenCV 2.x's Smooth implementations; the README names no specific mechanism beyond SIMD optimisation.
